Labéna beliefs.
Religious ideas,

Properly speaking, the Labénas have no caste religion. Some
worship devi or a deity, others a eati, while a good many observe
the Sikh teaching, Isolated as they were from the Hindus in tho
beginning, they exhibit a total ignorance of their religious principles,

though they have adopted several Hindu customs, they have as

yet imbibed nothing of their religion, Generally they believe in the

of the wood, the nixies of the water, the eati and Holi and Mata

wis. They fally beliove in magic and charms such as tho oficacy
of mysterious characters written on a scrap of paper,

In each village a raised platform serves as the sthén ‘or templo of
the Devi, Here a disciple or hermit lives permanently and women
constantly resort to this sacred spot with whey in their hands which
thoy present to him and ask about the future,

‘The serpent is worshipped on the Gugga Nawmi in Gujrit, Women*
take a chiiri and four chapétis and go to the hole of m serpent, whero
the Bhat is present, The chiiri and chapitie aro given to the Bhi,
and cow's milk is poured into tho hole. This hole is called gugga oF
bimbia and is a fixed place outside tho village. ‘The Ditlas must. first
worship the gugga before other castes can do it, and this is because it
is believed that the serpent is their offspring.

‘The pipal is the sacred tree. On thothird day after marriage the
bride if bridegroom are taken to @ pipal tree, ie stem is decorated
with red colour and maulé thread. ‘Tho married couple turn round the
treo and, after bowing their heads, come away.

Religious ceremonies connected with agriculture,

‘The Léhalis observe cortain ceremonies of a religions nature: in cons
nection with the cultivation of their fields, A limd, who understands the
astrological books, names the auspicious day on which ploughing should
bo commenced (this day falls always between the sth and 22nd. of
May). After the fields have been ploaghed and sown, a procession.
goes round all the fields, preceded oy one or two limés and two drums,
some of the company carrying at the samo time several large religious
books on their backs, this done, the whole company sits down in the
fields near tho villages and feasts on cakes nd chang supplied jointly
by all the land-holders. All this is done to secure the sprouting up of
the seeds sown, after that the water-covrse for irrigating the felde 4
repaired, on which occasion a sheep is offered up to the thd which is
supposed to have special caro of the watercourse. Again, a8 soon. as
the seeds hays sprouted, another ceremony is performed ; this consists
in sticking small branches of the pencil-cedar here and there in the
field, and burning incense, while some mombers of the family eit down,
eat, oud drink a little, and murmur some prayers. ‘This is to ensure
that each geain which has sprung up may prosper and produce many
ears. When the fields are nearly ripe, a gout or sheep is killed in
honor of the thd, in several villages horse-races are held’ at the samo
time, Till the festival of the ripening grain has been celebrated, so,
body is allowed to out grass or any green thing with a sickle wade of
iron, as in such case the fiold-god would become angry and’ sond_ frost
to destroy or injure the harvest. If, therefore, a ‘Labuli wants
before the harvest encrifice, ho must out it with tho sickle made of the
hom of an ox or sheep, or fear it off with the hand. Infractions of
this role were formerly severely punished, at present a fine of one of
two rupees suffices, which goos into the pocket of the jégindér or the
illage headman, ‘The iron sicklo is used as soon as the harvest hag
‘eon declared to be commenced by the performance of the sacrifice.

‘that the universal degeneracy of mankind has so increased in compari=

enter into living bodies and men’s virtues are rarely great enough to

Ataboy’s wedding Mihnghs observe no ceremony in their own
house, but collect a few leading members of the brotherhood and go
to the house of the girl’s father, accompanied by the bridegroom,
‘There they perform some of the necessary ceremonies and the next day
bring the girl to their own house. On the following morning the
menbers of the brotherhood carry the bridegroom and the bride to a
‘malah or mulberry tree, under which they seat the couple. A long
thread mauli is wrapped round the stem of the tree and all present,
together with the couple walk seven times round it, Afterwards a
quantity of churma (loaves of bread and pounded sugar) is distributed
tothe assembly, After this they return home and are fed sumptuously
at the expense of the bridegroom's father.

Ibbotson (§ 527) writing of the Dam and Mirdsi observed that. Déim
is tho Hindu and Indian while Mirdsi is the Musulmén and Arabic
namo (ofthe caste), the whole class being commonly called Dim-Mirdsi
by tho people. But the collocation of the two uames docs not
appear to imply that the two groups are necessarily identical or even
equal. They are loosely coupled together in popular speech, just as
aro Chéhyé.Chamér and Mochi-Julihé, in a manner which only’ sorves
to conceal the fact that the Dim-Mirdsi group includes sub-groups of
varying status. It may be conjectured that the Mirisi is a kind of
promoted Dém, elevated by function above his parent group. Ibbetson
no doubt observed that the Diims must be carefully distinguished from
tho Dom or Doma, the executioner and corpse-burner of Hindustan,
and the type of all uncleanliness to « Hindu ; as also from the Dim of
tho Hill States whom he classed as Diimna and not as Mirdsi, the term
Dim being understood to wean in the Himalayan area a worker in
bamboo. But it is probably safer to regard the Dom, Dém, Démna
sud Domra are mere synonyms, all four being of pretty much the same
status, though not necessarily of the same origi. Functionally the
‘Mirési is certainly the Muhammadan equivalent of the Hindu Bhat.
“Bvon Jifs,’ wrote Ibbetson, ‘ompley Mirésis, though the hereditary
genealogist of many of the Jét tribes is the Sénsi, and Réjputs often

castes, is exceodingly low, but he attends at weddings and on similar
Secasions to recite goneslogios. Moreover there aro grades evon among
Mirdsis.” ‘This is eminently trac. Who social position of the Mirésr
like that of the Bua, depends on several factors, his function, hig
origin and bis means. Like all the client or parasite classes’ the

nently attached to a Réjput clan and boneficed by it, ranks higher than

History.

In 1586 A. D. the Mohmands end other tribes of the Ghoria Khel in
the neighbourhood of Peshéwar, having made Jaléla the Rosmivia their
leader, revolted against the Mughals and invested the fort of
(Peshawar) killing Sayyid Hamid the faujdér when he sallied forth
‘Sgainst thom,

‘Tho Tarakzai clan and its chiefs played a considerable part in tho
history of the frontier in the Abdali period. Zain Khén, its chief, was
sipih-silér ands great noble at the court of Ahmad Shih. After the
conquest of Dehli by that monarch he held the Sababdérship of
Sirhind. His grandson Arsalin Khén was also chief, but he rebelled
against Taimér Shh and succeeded in gaining over the Afridis and
other Afghén tribes. With their aid ho roturned to Dhika, which he
had abandoned, and closed the Khaibar to Taimir Shéh’s forces,
levying toll on caravans on his own account. But he was induced
to go to the Darréni court undor » safe-conduct and was there
imprisoned and eventually tied to the fore-fect of an elephant and
crushed to death, in 1792,

‘The Mohmands have always been distracted by internal feuds, The
Baezai under Dindér Khin were at fond with the Tarakzai under
‘Arsalin Khén, each having slain the other’s father.

Ziérats and shrines in the Mohmand country

Ninxi-, or Nixof-xi-rawri.—A sect which in 1805 appears to havo attracted
‘a considerable number of converts, principally in the Districts of
Gurgéon, Rohtak and Hissér. It derived its origin from a woman,
named Nénki, the wife of one Dharm Dis, of Nérnaul, who eloped with
a Brahman named Dedh R4j. Dedh Réj and Nénki travelled to Bengal,
where, said, they learnt the doctrines now observed by their
followers. They returned to Kanaund about 1850 and commenced
proselytising. The villago cf Chisena in Khotri was the head-
quarters of the panth, and there they built a temple containing a metal
image of Neh Kulunk, whose incarnation Dedh R6j pretended to be.
he Hindu Shastras foretell tho advent of Neh Kulank towards the
close of the world’s history, when mankind shall have become exceed-
ingly corrupt, a belief almost identical with that of the Muhammadans
in their expected Imam Mabdi, Dedh Réj is said to have written
three works explanatory of his doctrines. He appears to bave incnl-
cated tho abolition of caste; intermarriage irrespective of class or
position in life; and a more unrestrained intercourse betwoon the
sexes. Converts were initiated by Dedh Xéj, who used to give
them a swootmeat to eat, which was supposed to awaken a religious
fronzy. Afterwards, like the Kikas, they received a cotton or woollen
rosary. At prayer meetings the Nénki-ké-pnnth is assembledia a
line, chanted verses moving their bodies to and fro till they worked
themselves into great excitement, when they danced and ranted. Truth
was a virtue strongly inculcated by Dedh Raj and his followers. The
parents of this sect died about 1865 and Bhagarith Dfs, a brother of
Dedh Réj, became its recognized head. The Nanki-ké-panth observed
many of the Hindu festivals ; and except in matters of caste, held no
‘very new ideas.

Houses and villages.—Dwellings aro usvally constructed of stone in

living rom, The uppormost is a tower for defence, though sometimes
it is only an open verandah on the roof, where the women sit and spin,
In many casos thoro is only one room in each storey, in which ease all
the inmates sleep together. In the houdes of the richer classes there aro

under ground. Orakzai villages generally of houses built

Birth,* naming, and cirewmcision.—A pregnant woman among the
poorer classes does not desist from her menial duties of bringing gross
‘and wood from the hills until the last month of her pregnaney, when sho
generally remains at home. The period of confinement is very short,
nd child-birth is asa rale easy among these tribes. After delivery
the lying-in woman remains in bed for only thres days, but she refrains
from doing any work for a week, After the lapse of forty days she
resumes her usual occupations, No notice is taken of the birth of
female child, but the advent of a boy is made tho oceasion of rejoicing,
Droms are beaten by Dims, who reosive a present of Rs. 5 (Kébuli)
and gur and raisins, to the value of from Rs. 2 to 8, aro distributed
among the friends, who come to congratulate the family. Among the

strictions of the Mulléhs, who taboo thie form of amusement, but it still

Betrothal and marriage—As a rule among the Orakzais, children
are not betrothel “until they attain puberty, and marriage quickly
follows betrothal. Marriages are usually determined by consider
ations of family convenience. It is a common practice for a man
to mary his first cousin, in which case an exchange of betrothal
is generally effected. ‘Tho rasména for marriages between. relations
fixed at from Rs, 100 to Rs. 240 (Kébuli). Besides this, food, clothes
and ornaments have to be supplied. ‘The quantity of food to’ be sup:
plied, which consists of ghi, rice, gur, maize, wheat, mung, salt and
henna, varies according to the number of guests to be fed. Clothes to
the value of Rs, 10 and ornaments worth Rs, 60 are also furnished,
When a girl is not married to one of her kinsmen, the following
arrangements are made preliminary to the betrothal. Some women of
the boy’s family first visit the houge of the gi:!’s relations, and return
after satisfying themaclves as to tho suitability of the match, Overs
tures aro then made by the boy's family, and, if these aro favourably
received, the marriage settlements are made. Some elders from the
boy's village, accompanied by a few women of his family, next. proceed
to the girl’s house oa a night appointed for the purpose, and the terms
of the marriage settlement are announced. This deputation, which
is feasted at the expense of tho boy’s parents with gur or, in the caso
of mell- todo people, with goat's meat, generally sucaseds in procuring
some reductionof the rasmidna demanded for the girl, which varies
from Rs. 200 to 700 (Kébuli) according to éhe position of the parties
nd the attractions of the girl, Rs, 300 being the usual amoudt Te

Inheritance —The rale of primogeniture does not obtain, all the sone
Deing entitled to an equal share in their father’s property. The
father has a right to will away his whole property to one son to tho
exclusion of the rest, but this is very rarely done. All tho sons are
bound to join in the funeral expenses of their father, and, if any
fails to do so, his share of the property, moveable and immoveable,
is reduced by this amount Tho rules regarding succession are
generally the sume across the border as in British territory, devolation
Of property being regulated on the pagwand system. ‘The ovly
important difference is that a widow has no interest in her deceased
husband's property, which devolves integrally on the next of kin,
whose transferable property she becomes. If she is young and attrac-
tive, the heir weds her himself, or “marries her either to one of his
relations, or to an outsider. If sho is old; and without any marketable
value, sho is maintained by the heir, and in retura is hound to perform
hous-hold duties. ‘There is a curious custom, however, in vogue
among the Khadizais, under which women have equal shares with
men in the property of a deceased relation.

‘The tenures among the Pathéns of Dir, Swat and Béjuur are strongly

to their political systems. When the country was first oocu-
jied all lands were divided into tappas between the septs of the tribe.
h teppa was further divided into daftars, one to eagh biol gud cach
daftar was further subdivided into brakhas or bakhras, the individual
shares. Any person possessing a share, however small, in a daftar is
called a daftari, and in order to equalise the shares of each daftari, as
far as possible, the lands of each khel were classed according to the
nature of the soil into rands or wands each bearing some distinctive
local name. ‘Thus. daftari’s share was not necessarily a compact piece
of land, but was often composed of scattered plots in several wands
Tt was calculated by somo recognised unit of measurement, which varied
in different localities, such as pticha, rupaiya, paisa, tura, ghonaye,
nimkai, tirao, pao, ete.

Part of the land of the community used, however, to be excluded
from pie pert, and allotted to the use of those who had served the
Khel or village by sword or prayer. Such land is called seri and is ex-
empt from redistribution or khassure which otherwise universal,
save in Sam Rénfzai. Seri lands are beld sometimes by a powerful
Khén, sometimes for the use of the village or tribal jirga, bat more fre-

yuently by the village mulla or some member of the priestly classes.
aes tule, they lie ou the border between two communities, or are
Jands in dispute, and thus form buffers between villages. ‘The periodical
redistribution occurs every 5, 10, 15 or 20 years, and extends to the
lands of whole septs, occasionally even to the tappas, while exchange of
the jars of khels and individuals is univ It says much for the
discipline of the community that redistributic accomplished down to
the smallest fraction of a sub-share of each lividual share. At the
‘end of the Ist year the whole khel casts lots for and redistributes all
the rice lands: at the end of the 2nd year this is repeated: at the end
of the 3rd fresh lots are cast for the rice lsnds and also for the double-
‘erop rain lands: in the 4th year lots are cast again for the rice lands
‘also for the single-crop rain lands: and st the end of the 5th year
lots aro cast for the rico lands slono, At the end of the 6th year’ the
Khel moves off en bloc toa new daftar. The results are disastrous as
no one has the slightest interest in improving the land, developing irrt-
tion or building permanent houses, No orchards, no gardens, few,
if apy, trees save in the sacred precincts of a zidrat exist, .

case of the Thakksrs, who are here at tho bottom of the scale, and
amongst whom the deterioration of race and generally dwindling ten-
dency are most marked. The daughters leave the clan, and the men
must cither remain unmarried or take their brides from sub-tribes
which, though not regarded consanguinous, have so frequently in-
Yermavried during past contaries as to ruin the physical prospects of
the progeny. On embracing Islém the strict rules of the marriago
Jaw are much released, and though outside marriages are preferred,
there is nothing to prevent general marriages even within the clan. AS
a consequence we find that, while the Muhammadin Manhés, Katil and
Selehria Réjputs have so multiplied, as to have reduced their aver-
‘age holding 7 acres in Shakargarh, the Hindu have dwindled until each
proprietor owns as much as 18 acres, and in the case of the lower clans
the contrast ia much more striking.”

‘THE RAJPUT GROUPS AND THEIR ORIGINS,

‘The Réjpats of the Panjab may be broadly grouped, as Tbbetson
grouped them, into four territorial groups. First cote be Réjpnia of
the Delhi Territory and the Jumne valley, for the most part belonging
to the two great tribes of Tinwar and Chauhén which gave Delhi ita
most famous dynastin, "Next como the Réjputs of the river valleys
of the Western Plains, many of them hardly or not at all to be dis-
tinguished from Jéts and belonging for the most part to tho Bhatti
of Jaisalmer and Bikéner, and their predecessors the Panwér. ‘The
third group is the Rajput of the westem hills, including the Salt
Henge, including both dominant tribes of proud position such ae the
Janjas and Mongul Réjputs from the Jammu hills, and descendants
either of YadGbansi (Bhatti) dynasty of Kashmir and the mythical
Réjé Rasélu of Sidlkot, so famous in Panjab folklore, or of @ group of
tribes, apparently of Punwdr origin, which now hold the hills on either
bank of the Jhelam. Finally we have the Réjpute of the Kingra
Lills of whom the Katoch may be taken as the type, so ancient
their very origin. end advent. to their present abodes are lost in the
fasts and the Réjputs of the lower hills which fringe the Punjab

“The Réyhis and Thékars or ‘Thakkars, are found in the oater hills

‘and their great numerical importance and wide distribution seom te
indicate that, for a very lony period, they have been settled in the hills,
In origin they are generally regarded as being the result of an amal

tion of the castes above and below them but it seems hardly poseiblo
that such » large community con have como into existence wholly in
this way. A moro probable explanation is given by Sir J. B. Lyall, "Ho
says:— "There it an idea current in the hills that of the landholding
castes, the Thékurs, Réthis, Kanets and Ghirthe aro either indigenoes
to the hills, or indigenous by tho half blood ; and that tho Bralimans,
Rejpals aud ‘others aro the desendnts of invaders and eetilor from
‘the plains.” ‘This popalar idea probably gives us tho clue to the trae
ae the Thékars and Réthis. It is algo in keeping with a common

meaning: ‘The Chanél is the elder brother ; the Réthi the younger.”
The signification attached to this eaying by the people is that the bigh

brother ison an elder one. No ceremony of any importance can take
place without their nce and help—at births, marriages and deaths
they are indispensable in oue enpacity or another. It seems improb-
able, however, that this was the original signification, which has be-
‘come obscured through the lepeo of ages. It is more likely that the
seying is an unconscious expression of the general conviction that the
Chanils were the original inhabitants of the hills. ‘The Réqhis came at
fa later period ; yet so long a time has passed since even they migrated

“There can be little doubt that, asa hill tribe, they are older than
the Brahmans and Réjputs, who came from the plains at a later period ;
‘and we may safely conclade that the oldest strata among them are
escended, either directly or by the hulf blood, from the early Aryan
colonists of the hills, The first Aryan immigrants, as we now know,
intermarried freely with the aborigines, resulting in a fusion of the two
races from which may have sprung the various low custe tribes now
forming such sn important pert of the population. Bat the complete.
ness of the fusion was not at all times uniform, and later waves of
immigration may have remained more or lees isolated, forming the
nnoleus of the community which now comprises the Thékurs and Réhis.
Bat while this was probably tho origin of the tribes it is certain that
general opinion regarding them is also well founded. ‘That they
have received large uccessions from the other castes by defections from
the Brshmans end Réjputs and by amalgamation of theso castes with
the Sudras, is hardly open to doubt. This is the general belief among
themsclves’ and_ their family traditiors all tend to confirm it. We may
therefore regard the Thékurs and Réthis as being now a conglomerate
people, representing the ultimate product of the welding together of
many different contributions to their ranks.

this classification does not cover the whole order: seo infra under ashes,

Soorat Customs,

Birth—The birth of a son is annoanced by the firing of guns, Sheep
are slaughtered and the meat distributed on the third day, asa role, in
the mosque or village chauk. ‘The infant recoives its name on the third
day, as a role, snd in exceptional casos on the seventh day. ‘The child
is named either by the eldest male momber of the family or by some
friend nominated by the father. ‘The bdng or formula of faith is not
repeated in tho child’s ear as is the case with other Muhammadans,
The child is generally given a cap or turban to wear after he bas com:
pleted his seventh year. Circumcision is, as rule, performed when
the child is ton years old. No rejoicings of any kind take place on
the bitth of a female child.

Batrothal,—On the child’s attaining the age of paberty the father
looks ont for a suitable match for him. ‘The father or legal guardian of
the girl sought in marriage fixes the amount for which he is willing to
hostow her hand, and if the partion agroe, tho contract is made, Should
difference atiso mutual friends aro called in to use their good offices
and bring about a settlement. Some Rs. 8 or 4 aro generally paid as
enrnest-money, the balance beiag given afterwards. The marriage,
however, cannot be celetrated antil the whole amount is paid up. An
exchange of girls is also somotimes effected, in which case no money is
passed on either side, ‘Tho Shirénnfs have a sayiog that by receiving
money for their danghtera they sell their flosh, but not the bones, or in
othar words, that the: hasband is entitled to chastise his wife or inflict _
any bodily injary apon her, bat is not at liberty to kill her. ‘Te amount

Marriage-—The marriage is not celobrated until the betrothed
partios are fully grown up, or generally until the bridegroom is 20 and
the bride 16 years of age. An exception to this rule is said to be
unknown, ‘The relations and friends of the couple are invited to the

tribute thefr quota to the marriage feast. In return they are given
a lungi or Rs. 3 or 4in oash onleaving, ‘The drum and sarangi are the
only instraments used on the occasion,

Funeral ceremonies.—These are the samo as are in vogue amongst
Muhommadans generally, with a few unimportant exceptions :—

(8) No alms are given to the poor onthe 7th or 40th day after

Inheritance.—On the death of the father his sons are considered his
legal heirs and divide his property equally amongst them. The eldest,
however, is usually given a slightly larger share, In default of male
issue, the brother, or nephew, ot any direct descendant in the male ti
succeeds. In case of failure of any such direct heir, all the male
members of the branch to which the deceased belonged divide the

property equally between them. Tho females of the family are not
entitled to anything,

Bight of —An offender who is unable to protect himself from
his enemy or, in other words, when his own territory is too hot to hold
him, generally takes refuge with a chief or other powerful personage
Delonging to some other section or tribe. Thy custom (nahora it 18
called) is to take a sheep and slaughter it at the door of the person's
house whose protection is claimed, and who is bound to give him refuge.
‘The offender then becomes the protector’s hamedya or neighbour, and
is bound to make good to the latter any loss incurred by him in
consequence of the responsibility he has undertaken. In the event of
the hamsdya’s death the protecto:’s claim forms the first charge on the
deceased's property. Another method of claiming protection consists
in the offender's tying the end of his chddar to that of the wife of some
powerful personage, when the lator generally affords him the suecour

he requires, though he is not bound to do 80 as in the former case,
‘The eustom of nahora is also employed when one man begs any great
favour of another, The slaughtering of a sheep at a person's door
marks the urgenoy of the case, and is something like the Hindu custom
of sitting dharna,

Rajputs and some other classes ef, Panyjiébi Dicty., p. 1087. At initie

cccasionally an entirely new name is taken, e.g. Rém Uhand may be-

whose name is Singh may be changed into the dynastic sufix of Sain,
Parkish, etc. Singh is comparatively seldom used as a royal affix.
It is assumed in Bashahr at the naming ceremony and is not changed
at soceeion, In Ohatnbe too it in not Ghaugod, at, both’ betore ead
after accession, the ancient suffix Varma is used instead of Singh by
the priests when the ruling chief is referred to by namo in any
religious ceremony. In several states, ag. Kulu, it has in modern
times replaced the much more ancient ‘Pél,” As a Réjpat affix ‘ Singh’
‘only appears to havo come into goneral use in tho 16th century. A
syncopated form of Singh appears in clan names ending in -si, each as
Wairsi, Bhégsi, Barsi, ‘This syncopated suffix is common in
Réjputéne and Central Indis, Seo also under Shin.

Phe observances of the Sulténis,—The village shrines of Sarwar aro

and collecting offerings. ‘These offerings, which are generally in small
change or small handfuls of grain or cotton, are maiuly presented by

rot is made by placing dough to the extent vowed on hot piece of
earth, where a fire has been burning, and distributing it when baked.
A special rot ceremony is also performed once a year on a Friday in
most Salténi families, A huge loaf is cooked containing a kaccha
mannd of flour and half a kaccha maund of gur. ‘The Bharai attends
and beats.the dram, and sings the praises of the saint while it is
preparing. When it is ready he gets a quarter and the family with
their neighbours eat the rést, ‘The saint is ale worshipped by sleeping
on the ground instead of on a bed; this is called chauk bharnd.
Wrestling matches (ching béjéni) aro also held in his honour, and the
offerings made to the performers go towards keeping up the shrine
at Nigéha. A true worshipper of Sultén too will not sell milk on
Thursday ; he will consame it himself or give it away, but will not
sell it,

Sarwar is essentially a saint of the Jéts, and the worship of Sarwar,
which is, I believe, practically unknown outside the Punjab, is within
that Province the prevalent cult of the central or Jat districts. ‘Tho
Ihinwars, Gujars and the lower castes generally are also devoted to this
saint: but among the women who are his chief worshippers even

inthe month of Séwan. In the Delhi territory the saint is not popular
asin tho Panjab proper, but still, according ‘to Ibbetson, he is even
there ‘ generally worshipped ; shrines in his honour are common ; vows
and pilgrimages to him are frequent, and Brabmans tie threads on the
wrists of their clients ona fixed date in his namo,”

Anybody of any caste, even a Chamér, may call himself a
orshipper of Sarwar, and persons of all religions and all castes, more
expecially the Jéts and Jhfawars, are his followers. ‘The saint confined
himself to performing miracles and seems never to baye deviated into
susthing approaching to a verbal creed or doctrine, or even to a compo.
sition of any kind, and consequently his following is larger than that of
most saints in the Province, ‘The Saltdnf may reverencs the Prophet, or
he may worship Devi and the $8 crores of Hindu deities without ceasing
to bea Sulténi. He may smoke es much as he likes and dross his
hair as he pleases. The only observance which distingnishes Sarwar’s
Hindn followers from the ordinary Hindus is that they will not eat the
‘meat of animals which have been killed by jhatka or a blow on the back
of the neck. The Sulténf, if ho cats meat at all, must ent animals
‘whose throat has been eut in the orthodox Musalinén manner. ‘This
Serounts for the fact that comparatively few Sikhs are fllowars of

The Darwosh are par excellence Waztrs being called Ster Waxir,
or great Wazirs, and the MahsGds are in every respect their inferiors,

Soctau Customs,

Dress,-Mon wear a white or dark bluo pagri, and an angratha
(eharai in Pashto) or a shirt, embroidered on the collar and front. with
noedle-work of silk and cotton, and a pair of loose tronsers (shalwfr),
usually made of strong white cotton cloth, Sandals are usually worn,

 

‘Women wear a gown (kamis) hanging loose to the fect, of chintz
omamented about the neck and front with silken needlework: shalwar
made of imported cloth: and sandals but seldom shoes The similarity
between men and women in dress is noticeable,

‘Women observe no parda, weat no voils and mix freely with the
‘men when administering to their wants. Hospitality is a primo virtuo
‘and guests are welcomed by both men and women: for tho latter the
guests frst set aside a portion of the food provided by tho host:
thie foaled tho des share, Tho Mabsds boast that thoy ‘have no

‘man amongst them, Whenover a family is brought low by deaths,
Tecidents, or raids from without, the clan subscribes to re-establish
it, one bringing « bullock, another a blanket, and so on,

 

Marriage—The Mahsid marriage customs aro similar to those of
other Wazirs. ‘The price of s woman ranges from Hs. 60 to 150.
‘The marringo procession, which goes from the bridegroom's house to
fetch the bride, consists of 100 to 200 young men, and 50 to 60 women
or young girls, who have two orthree drums with them. ‘The women
sing songs, and the young men dance, waving in their hands their
swords and shields, and others fire off their matchlocks. They also
take with them two or three sheep, or a bullock, with a quantity of
rice, Ono or two spend the whole night in noisy rejoicing. Next
morning the procession returns to its own village, taking in its midst
the bride, who is mounted on amare. The marriage service is read
by the mullah after an interval of fifteen to twonty days, the bride
groom and tho bride having no intercourse in the meanwhile. ‘The bride
{Sin this way brought to her husband’s houso before her marriage
merely to become acquainted with his family. A woman whose hus
bands invariably die is called akhraba sheza or a ‘ scorpion-like? woman,

  

  

 

   

  

—Mourning consists in wailing and beating thy breasts, in which
‘Mullahs wash the body snd prepsroit for the coffin,
the grave is dug by the young men of the village.

Qn returoing from the graveyard the relatives and friends of the
deceased are entertained by men of @ different section of the tribe
to their own.

for centuries, Mshséds are slack in 1s duties. They have
charms (ida), and apperoctly the Michan Khol havo many Kinds of
charms.” ‘The Akhwunds practise cures by blowing. All Waafrs,
